wichtigste: The Coriolis force is an inertial force, that is, an apparent force.
The Coriolis parameter is f = 2Ω·sin φ.
At the equator the horizontal Coriolis force is zero, at the poles it is greatest.
In the Northern Hemisphere it deflects to the right, in the Southern Hemisphere to the left.
In the geostrophic wind, the pressure gradient force and the Coriolis force balance each other.
It is named after Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis, who described it in 1835.

abschnitte.text: The **Coriolis force** only appears in a **rotating frame of reference** such as the Earth. Seen from outside, a body moves straight ahead while the Earth keeps turning beneath it. To an observer on the Earth, it looks as if the body is being deflected. That is why it is called an **inertial force** or **apparent force**. It was described in 1835 by the French physicist **Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis** in a paper about rotating machines.

The strength of the horizontal deflection is described by the **Coriolis parameter** f = 2Ω·sin φ. Here Ω is the angular velocity of the Earth, about 7.29 · 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹, and φ is the latitude. At the **equator**, sin 0° equals 0, so there is no horizontal deflection there. At the **poles**, f is greatest. At 45° latitude you get f = 2 · 7.29 · 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹ · 0.707, about **1.0 · 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹**. Switzerland lies close to 46° latitude, so the value is very similar.

In the **Northern Hemisphere**, moving air is deflected to the **right** of its direction of motion. In the **Southern Hemisphere** the sign of f is negative, and the deflection is to the **left**. That is why low-pressure areas turn anticlockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere. According to **Buys Ballot's law**, if you stand with your back to the wind in the Northern Hemisphere, the low lies to your **front left**. It is shifted forwards because of friction with the ground.

In the free atmosphere, high above the ground, there is hardly any friction. There the **pressure gradient force** and the **Coriolis force** balance each other. The wind that results is called the **geostrophic wind**. It does not blow straight from the high into the low, but **parallel to the isobars**, the lines of equal air pressure. That is why weather maps are easy to read: isobars that are close together mean strong wind.

The Earth's rotation can be made visible with a **Foucault pendulum**. The plane in which it swings seems to turn slowly, because the Earth is turning beneath it. At the **North Pole**, a full turn takes about one **sidereal day**, about 23 hours 56 minutes. At middle latitudes it takes longer, because the effect decreases with the sine of the latitude. At the equator the plane of swinging does not turn at all.

gewusst: The Coriolis force is far too weak to decide which way water spins down the plughole of a bath; other influences decide that.
Léon Foucault demonstrated his famous pendulum in Paris in 1851.

teile.einleitung: A greenhouse, also called a glasshouse, is a house made of glass or see-through plastic. Inside it, plants grow protected and warm, even when it is still cool outside.
wichtigste: Greenhouse and glasshouse mean the same thing.
The walls are made of glass or see-through plastic.
Sunlight comes in, and the warmth stays inside.
In Switzerland, tomatoes, for example, are often grown in greenhouses.
On hot days the windows are opened so that it does not get too hot.
Certain gases in the air act in a similar way to the glass: this is the greenhouse effect.

abschnitte.text: A **greenhouse** or **glasshouse** is a house in which plants are grown in the warmth. Its walls and roof are made of **glass** or see-through **plastic**. This lets in a lot of sunlight, which the plants need to grow. There are small greenhouses in gardens and huge ones on vegetable farms.

The **sunlight** shines through the glass and warms the soil and the plants. The warm air can hardly escape through the glass. That is why it is warmer in a greenhouse than outside. Exactly the same thing happens in a **car** that stands in the sun in summer with its windows closed. It gets very hot inside. That is why you must never leave children or animals in a car.

**Tomatoes** like it warm. That is why in Switzerland they are often grown in greenhouses. Cucumbers, peppers, lettuce and herbs grow there too. A greenhouse is especially useful in **spring**, when it is still cold outside. You can sow early in the year, and the young plants are protected from frost.

In strong sunshine it can get too hot in a greenhouse. Then the plants suffer. That is why a gardener opens the **windows** on hot days. Fresh air cools things down. Large greenhouses often have automatic ventilation, shade nets and watering systems.

The Earth also has a kind of glass roof. Certain **gases** in the atmosphere, for example carbon dioxide and water vapour, hold back heat. This is called the **greenhouse effect**. Without it, it would be very cold on Earth. When people release more of these gases into the air, the Earth gets warmer.

gewusst: Without the natural greenhouse effect, the average temperature on Earth would be far below zero degrees.
Some botanical gardens have huge glasshouses in which rainforest plants grow.

teile.einleitung: Global warming is the rise in the average temperature on Earth since the beginning of industrialisation. The main cause is greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane, which people release mainly by burning coal, oil and natural gas. The effects can be felt in Switzerland too, for example in melting glaciers.
wichtigste: Since industrialisation, the global temperature has risen by a good 1 °C.
Before industrialisation, the CO2 content of the air was around 280 ppm.
Over 100 years, methane has an effect about 28 times stronger than CO2.
Since 1988, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) has summed up the state of climate research.
The Paris Agreement of 2015 aims to keep warming well below 2 °C, if possible at 1.5 °C.
Switzerland is warming more than the average because land areas warm up faster than oceans.
Sea level is rising because water expands and ice on land melts.

abschnitte.text: Burning coal, oil and natural gas produces **carbon dioxide** (CO2). Before industrialisation, the CO2 content of the air was around 280 ppm; today it is over 420 ppm (as of about 2025). On top of this comes **methane** from livestock farming, rice fields and natural gas leaks, which over 100 years has an effect about 28 times stronger than CO2. These gases strengthen the **greenhouse effect** and hold back more heat in the atmosphere.

The **Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC)** was founded in 1988 and sums up the results of thousands of studies. According to its reports, it is clear that humans are causing the warming. The years since 2015 are among the warmest since measurements began. Important data come from weather stations, satellites, buoys and ice cores.

**Sea level** is rising because warm water expands and ice on land melts. Heatwaves, droughts and heavy rain are becoming more frequent or stronger. Many coral reefs are bleaching, and some kinds of animals and plants have to move to cooler areas. Low-lying island states and coastal cities are especially affected.

Since pre-industrial times, Switzerland has warmed about twice as much as the global average. The reason is that **land areas** warm up faster than oceans. According to the **GLAMOS** network, the glaciers lost around 10 per cent of their volume together in the record years 2022 and 2023. There are fewer days with snow, and thawing permafrost is making some mountain slopes unstable.

abschnitte.titel: What is being done about it
abschnitte.text: In the **Paris Agreement** of 2015, almost all countries agreed to keep warming well below 2 °C, if possible at 1.5 °C. To do this, greenhouse gas emissions must fall sharply until **net zero** is reached. In 2023, Swiss voters approved the Climate and Innovation Act, which aims for net zero by 2050. In everyday life it also helps to save energy, travel by bike and train and waste less.

begriffe.erklaerung: A gas in the air that holds back heat, for example CO2 or methane.
Parts per million, used to measure tiny amounts of a gas in the air.
The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, which sums up knowledge about climate change.
No more greenhouse gas is released than is removed from the air again.

gewusst: Ice cores show that today's CO2 content of the air is the highest for at least 800,000 years.
Swiss researchers at the University of Bern have studied important ice cores from Antarctica.
In summer 2022, the freezing level over Switzerland was at times above 5,000 m.

teile.einleitung: On 28 May 2025, the Birch Glacier above Blatten in the Lötschental broke off. A huge mass of ice and rock buried a large part of the village, which had been evacuated beforehand thanks to good monitoring.
wichtigste: Blatten is the village furthest up the Lötschental in Valais.
Rockfalls from the Kleines Nesthorn loaded the Birch Glacier with debris.
On 19 May 2025, around 300 people were evacuated from Blatten.
Before it broke off, the glacier sped up to around 10 metres per day.
Experts call the event a rock and ice avalanche.
The debris dammed the River Lonza into a lake.

abschnitte.text: **Blatten** is the village furthest up the **Lötschental**. The valley is a side valley on the north side of the Rhône Valley in the canton of Valais. High above the village lies the **Birch Glacier**, below the Kleines Nesthorn. The **Lonza** flows through the valley.

abschnitte.titel: A glacier under a heavy load
abschnitte.text: From mid-May 2025, masses of rock kept breaking loose from the **Kleines Nesthorn**. The debris stayed on the Birch Glacier and pressed heavily on it. The glacier then slid down the valley faster and faster. Measurements at the front of the glacier showed it speeding up from a few metres to around **10 metres per day**. Such an acceleration is seen as a typical warning sign before a collapse.

Experts watched the slope closely. On 17 May, part of the village was cleared. On **19 May 2025**, nine days before the collapse, the whole village with around **300 people** was evacuated. Animals were also taken to safety. In this way, the monitoring prevented a much bigger disaster.

On 28 May 2025 the glacier broke off. A mixture of glacier ice and rock crashed and flowed into the valley. Experts call this a **rock and ice avalanche**. The masses buried a large part of Blatten. The cone of debris blocked the valley and dammed the **Lonza**. Behind it a lake formed, which flooded more houses.

Villages further down were evacuated as a precaution, because people feared the water might suddenly break through. However, the Lonza gradually found its way through the debris. At the end of May, the canton had the sluice gates of the **Ferden reservoir** opened. In this way the empty reservoir could take in water and debris and pass them on.

gewusst: The Blatten event attracted attention all over the world because the warning came so early.
Radar devices, cameras and drones helped with the monitoring.

teile.einleitung: A doline is a funnel-shaped or bowl-shaped hollow in the ground. It forms in areas with easily dissolved rock such as limestone or gypsum. Such landscapes are called karst.
wichtigste: Dolines are hollows in karst areas.
A solution doline forms when rock is slowly dissolved from above.
A collapse doline forms when the roof of a hollow space caves in.
Dolines form in limestone, and especially quickly in gypsum.
Several dolines that have grown together make an uvala.
The word doline comes from Slovenian.

abschnitte.text: Rainwater takes up a little carbon dioxide from the air and the soil and so becomes slightly acidic. This means it can slowly dissolve **limestone**. **Gypsum** dissolves even more easily than limestone. That is why caves, cracks and hollows form in areas with such rock. These landscapes are called **karst**. Typical karst areas in Switzerland are in the **Jura** and in the **limestone Alps**.

In places where especially large amounts of water soak away, the rock is dissolved more strongly. The surface there sinks very gradually. This creates a bowl-shaped hollow, a **solution doline**. This process takes a very long time. Some areas are dotted with hundreds of such hollows.

Sometimes water dissolves a **hollow space** beneath the surface. If the roof above it becomes too thin, it caves in. A steep funnel forms, a **collapse doline**. This can happen suddenly. That is why dolines can be dangerous for **houses and roads**, because buildings or roadways can sink.

At the bottom of a doline there is often a **swallow hole**, also called a **ponor**. There a stream suddenly disappears into the ground and flows on underground. If several neighbouring dolines grow together, a larger, irregular hollow forms. It is called an **uvala**.

The word **“doline”** comes from **Slovenian**. There “dolina” means valley or hollow. Many technical words for karst come from the **Karst plateau** in Slovenia. These landforms were studied there early on. The word karst itself also goes back to this region.

gewusst: In karst areas there are often hardly any streams on the surface, because the water disappears underground.
The word uvala also comes from a South Slavic language.

teile.einleitung: The mantle is the thickest layer of the Earth and lies between the Earth's crust and the core. It reaches down to a depth of about 2900 km and makes up most of the Earth's volume. Although it is solid almost everywhere, its rock flows very slowly.
wichtigste: The mantle lies beneath the Earth's crust and goes down to about 2900 km.
It makes up about two thirds of the Earth's mass.
The upper mantle is made mainly of the rock peridotite.
The mantle is mostly solid, but over long periods it can slowly change shape.
Heat currents move the rock in the mantle by a few centimetres a year.
The boundary with the core is called the Gutenberg discontinuity.

abschnitte.text: The **mantle** begins below the Moho, that is, at a depth of 5 to 70 km depending on the place. It goes down to about 2900 km, where the core begins. It is divided into the **upper mantle** and the **lower mantle**. In between lies a transition zone at a depth of about 410 to 660 km.

The upper mantle is made mainly of **peridotite**, a greenish rock. Peridotite contains a lot of the mineral **olivine**, which is known as the gemstone peridot. Sometimes pieces of the mantle reach the surface through volcanoes or mountain building. In Switzerland, such mantle rocks can be found, for example, on the Totalp near Davos.

In the mantle, temperatures range from about 1000 °C at the top to about 4000 °C at the boundary with the core. Even so, the rock is **solid** almost everywhere, because the enormous pressure stops it melting. But over millions of years it changes shape like very stiff dough. Only in a soft zone beneath the lithosphere, the **asthenosphere**, is a small part melted.

Hot rock slowly rises, cools down and sinks again. This movement is called **mantle convection**, similar to water in a cooking pot. It is only a few centimetres a year fast, about as fast as fingernails grow. The currents help to move the **continental plates**.

Nobody has ever drilled down into the mantle. Researchers study it with **seismic waves**, which travel at different speeds depending on the rock. In this way, in 1913, Beno Gutenberg discovered the boundary with the core, which today is called the **Gutenberg discontinuity**. There certain waves stop, because the outer core is liquid.

begriffe.erklaerung: A greenish rock that makes up most of the upper mantle.
A cycle in which warm material rises and cold material sinks.
A soft zone in the upper mantle on which the tectonic plates glide.
The boundary between the mantle and the core, at a depth of about 2900 km.

gewusst: The mantle is so thick that it is greater than the distance from Zurich to Moscow.
The gemstone peridot is made of olivine, a typical mineral of the mantle.
The solid rock of the mantle flows about as fast as your fingernails grow.

teile.einleitung: Eutrophication means that a body of water contains too many nutrients. Then algae and water plants grow too much, and oxygen is missing in the depths. Many Swiss lakes were heavily over-fertilised in the 20th century and have recovered since then.
wichtigste: Eutrophication is the build-up of nutrients such as phosphorus and nitrogen in a body of water.
In most Swiss lakes, phosphorus limits the growth of algae.
In 1986 the ban on phosphate in laundry detergents came into force in Switzerland.
When dead algae are broken down, bacteria use up a lot of oxygen.
A clear lake poor in nutrients is called oligotrophic.
Lake Baldegg and Lake Sempach have been artificially aerated since the 1980s.

abschnitte.text: Algae and water plants need nutrients to grow, especially **phosphorus** and **nitrogen**. Through fertiliser from fields and through waste water, too much of them gets into the water. Then algae grow too much, and the water becomes cloudy and greenish. This process is called **eutrophication**. In freshwater lakes phosphorus is usually the scarce nutrient. That is why even a little extra phosphorus sets off strong growth of algae.

abschnitte.titel: Lack of oxygen in the depths
abschnitte.text: Dead algae sink to the bottom of the lake. There they are broken down by **bacteria**, which use up a lot of **oxygen** in the process. Especially in summer, when the warm surface water does not mix with the cold deep water, oxygen soon runs short in the depths. Fish and other animals can no longer live there. Experts divide lakes into **trophic levels**: from **oligotrophic**, that is, poor in nutrients and clear, through mesotrophic and eutrophic to hypertrophic.

In the past, **phosphates from detergents** were a main source of over-fertilisation. In 1986 the **ban on phosphate** in laundry detergents came into force in Switzerland. At the same time, many **sewage treatment plants** were built and extended. In the chemical treatment stage, they remove phosphate through **precipitation** with iron or aluminium salts. This creates compounds that hardly dissolve and settle out as sludge. After that, the phosphorus levels in many lakes fell clearly.

Some lakes recover only slowly. In **Lake Baldegg** and **Lake Sempach** in the canton of Lucerne, oxygen was missing in the deep water because of over-fertilisation. That is why they have been **artificially aerated** since the 1980s, with oxygen being added. At the same time, efforts are made to let fewer nutrients from farming get into the lakes. Many Alpine lakes, on the other hand, are naturally oligotrophic.

In **Lake Murten** and other lakes, the cyanobacterium **Planktothrix rubescens** can multiply strongly. It then colours the water reddish. It is popularly called the **Burgundy blood alga**. The name recalls a legend: after the Battle of Murten in 1476, the lake is said to have been red with the blood of the Burgundians.

gewusst: The word “eutrophic” comes from Greek and means “well fed”.
Cyanobacteria are often called blue-green algae, but they are not real algae; they are bacteria.

teile.einleitung: In the mountains, masses of rock can break off and crash down into the valley. Experts watch dangerous slopes with measuring instruments so that people can be warned in time.
wichtigste: Unstable slopes are monitored with extensometers, radar and GNSS stations.
An extensometer measures how much a crack in the rock opens.
Ground-based radar measures almost without a break, satellites only every few days.
Threshold values automatically set off alarms or road closures.
During the rockfall at Piz Cengalo in 2017, the village of Bondo had been evacuated in time thanks to monitoring.
At Brienz/Brinzauls, a drainage tunnel greatly slowed down the landslide.

abschnitte.text: Rock often moves slowly for a long time before it breaks off. Water, frost and disappearing **permafrost** weaken the rock. If you measure these movements, you can recognise a fall early. In Switzerland, cantons, the Confederation and research institutes monitor many dangerous slopes. This makes it possible to protect villages, roads and railway lines.

An **extensometer** bridges a crack with a measuring wire or rod. If the crack widens, the instrument shows the movement to a fraction of a millimetre. **GNSS stations** use satellite navigation such as GPS. They work out their position all the time and so show the direction and speed of the movement in three dimensions. A **ground-based radar** opposite the slope measures every few minutes or so and also detects small changes.

The measurements are linked to **threshold values**. If the speed or the width of the crack reaches a set value, systems set off warnings, traffic lights or closures. Experts also use calculation methods to make predictions. In Fukuzono's **inverse velocity** method, the inverse of the speed is plotted against time. If the line heads towards zero, the approximate time of the fall can be estimated.

Near **Randa** in the Matter Valley, about 30 million cubic metres of rock fell in two events in 1991. They buried the railway line and dammed the River Vispa. Since then the rock face has been monitored scientifically. In August 2017 about 3 million cubic metres of rock broke off **Piz Cengalo** in the Val Bregaglia. Eight hikers died, and debris flows reached Bondo. Thanks to monitoring and warnings, the village had been evacuated in time.

A whole slope is sliding beneath the village of **Brienz/Brinzauls** in the Grisons. To slow it down, a **tunnel system** more than two kilometres long was built. Water drains out of the slope through boreholes, and the water pressure in the rock falls. By the end of 2025 the movement had dropped from about 2.5 metres to a few centimetres a year.

gewusst: An extensometer can detect movements thinner than a hair.
Ground-based radar can also see through fog and measures at night.

teile.einleitung: A fold is a piece of rock whose layers have been bent. Folds form when layers of rock are pushed together from the side over millions of years. In Switzerland you can see them well in the Jura and in the Alps.
wichtigste: A fold in rock consists of bent layers of rock.
Layers fold when they are pushed together from two sides.
Layers of rock originally lie flat on top of each other.
A mountain range made of folded layers is called a fold mountain range.
The Alps were folded up when Africa and Europe collided.
Large folds take millions of years to form.

abschnitte.titel: Layers like the pages of a book
abschnitte.text: Many rocks form at the bottom of a sea. There sand, mud and lime settle layer by layer. At first the **layers of rock** lie flat on top of each other, rather like the pages in a book. Over a long time they turn into solid rock. Only later can forces inside the Earth bend these layers.

When layers of rock are **pushed together** from two sides, they cannot get out of the way. They bend upwards and downwards. This creates a **fold**. An upward arch is called an **anticline**, and a downward dip a **syncline**. You can try this with a tablecloth: if you push it together, waves form. But rock moves only very slowly, and large folds take **millions of years**.

When a great many layers are folded and pushed on top of each other, they pile up into mountains. Such mountain ranges are called **fold mountains**. The **Alps** are an example. They formed when the **African Plate** pushed against the **European Plate**. Huge packages of rock were folded and piled up. The Himalayas are also fold mountains.

In the north-west of Switzerland lies the **Jura**. It consists of long, folded ridges of **limestone**. That is why it is called the **Folded Jura**. In the Alps, folds can often be seen well on **steep rock faces**, where the rock is exposed. There you can sometimes make out the bent layers from far away. So if you go hiking, you can read the history of the Earth directly in the rock.

gewusst: In the Alps, fossils of sea creatures can be found on high peaks, because the rock once lay on the sea floor.
Some folds are so small that they fit in a hand specimen, while others are kilometres in size.

teile.einleitung: The Earth is surrounded by a magnetic field that reaches far out into space. It makes the compass needle point north and protects the Earth from particles from space. It is produced deep inside the Earth.
wichtigste: At the surface, the Earth's magnetic field is about 25 to 65 microteslas strong.
Today the axis of the field is tilted by about 10 degrees from the Earth's axis of rotation.
In physics terms, there is a magnetic south pole near the geographic North Pole.
The Arctic magnetic pole is moving from Canada towards Siberia.
Declination is the angle between magnetic north and geographic north.
Since 2013, ESA's Swarm mission has been measuring the field with three satellites.

abschnitte.titel: A magnet from inside the Earth
abschnitte.text: Most of the magnetic field is produced in the **outer core** of the Earth. There, liquid, hot iron flows. These movements create electric currents and with them a magnetic field. This process is called the **geodynamo**. In 1839 the mathematician **Carl Friedrich Gauss** showed with a mathematical analysis that the field comes mainly from inside the Earth. An old unit of magnetic flux density is also named after him.

The field is similar to that of a big **bar magnet**. Today its axis is tilted by about **10 degrees** from the Earth's axis of rotation. The north pole of a compass needle is attracted by the south pole of a magnet. That is why, in physics terms, there is a **magnetic south pole** near the geographic North Pole, even though it is called the Arctic magnetic pole. The compass needle does not point exactly to geographic north. This angle is called **declination** or magnetic variation.

At the Earth's surface the field is about **25 to 65 microteslas** strong. It is weakest at the equator and about twice as strong at the magnetic poles. A fridge magnet is a hundred to a thousand times stronger. The **inclination**, or dip, is the angle between the field lines and the horizontal. At the magnetic poles the field lines run vertically, so the inclination is **90 degrees**.

The magnetic poles do not stay in one place. Since the 19th century the Arctic magnetic pole lay in the north of **Canada**. Around the year 2000 it was moving at over 50 kilometres a year. Since then it has crossed the date line and is moving towards **Siberia**. Over the South Atlantic and South America the field is particularly weak. This area is called the **South Atlantic Anomaly**, and satellites receive more radiation there.

The magnetic field deflects charged particles from the Sun, the **solar wind**. Some particles get into the atmosphere at the poles and make it glow. This creates **auroras**. Since 2013, the three satellites of ESA's **Swarm** mission have been measuring the field from different heights. This makes it possible to tell apart the parts coming from the core, the crust, the oceans and the ionosphere.

gewusst: In the Earth's history the magnetic field has flipped many times, most recently about 780,000 years ago.
Some migratory birds can sense the Earth's magnetic field and use it to find their way.

teile.einleitung: In a thunderstorm, a bright flash of lightning is followed by a loud bang or a long rumble: thunder. It is the sound that lightning makes in the air. If you watch lightning and thunder, you can even work out how far away a thunderstorm is.
wichtigste: Thunder is made because lightning suddenly heats the air very strongly.
The hot air expands explosively, and we hear this as a bang.
Sound takes about 3 seconds to travel one kilometre.
The seconds between lightning and thunder divided by three give the distance in kilometres.
If lightning and thunder come almost at the same time, the thunderstorm is very close.
After the last thunder, stay under shelter for about another 30 minutes.

abschnitte.text: A flash of lightning is a huge electrical discharge. In a fraction of a second it heats the air in a narrow channel to many thousands of degrees, according to estimates up to about **30,000 degrees**. The air suddenly expands. This creates a **pressure wave** that travels as sound. We hear this sound as thunder.

Light is so fast that we see the lightning practically at once. **Sound** is much slower and takes about 3 seconds to travel one kilometre. If you count, for example, 9 seconds between lightning and thunder, the thunderstorm is about 3 kilometres away. If the crash comes almost at the same time, the lightning is striking only a few hundred metres away. Then it is high time to stay indoors.

A flash of lightning is often several kilometres long. The sound from the nearby parts of the flash arrives first, and the sound from the more distant parts later. That is why we often hear not a short bang but a long **rumble** or roll. Mountains and hills also throw the sound back, like an echo. That is why thunder can echo for an especially long time in the mountains.

If you can hear thunder, you are close enough to be struck by lightning. You are safest in a building or a car. Lightning can still strike even at the end of a thunderstorm. That is why you wait about **half an hour** after the last thunder before going outside again. In Switzerland, thunderstorms happen mainly in summer, but rarely also in winter, sometimes even while it is snowing.

In the past people could not explain thunder. The Germanic peoples believed in the thunder god **Donar**. The German word for Thursday, **“Donnerstag”**, is named after him. In the Norse legends from Scandinavia, the thunder god is called **Thor**. When he hurled his hammer, so people said, it thundered in the sky.

gewusst: The English word “Thursday” means Thor's day.
Thunderstorms in winter with snowfall are sometimes called thundersnow.

teile.einleitung: Diagenesis is the name for all the changes that a loose sediment goes through after it has been deposited, until it has become solid rock. In this way sand becomes sandstone and mud becomes mudstone. Diagenesis ends where metamorphism begins.
wichtigste: Diagenesis is the hardening of loose sediment into sedimentary rock.
In compaction, sediment is squeezed together and loses pore water.
In cementation, minerals that come out of solution glue the grains together.
Angular rubble turns into breccia, rounded pebbles into conglomerate.
The change from peat to lignite to hard coal is called coalification.
At about 150 to 200 °C, diagenesis turns into metamorphism.

abschnitte.text: Rivers, wind and sea constantly deposit **sediments**: sand, gravel, mud or lime mud. Over time more and more layers settle on top. Under a growing **load** and at moderate temperatures, the loose sediments become solid **sedimentary rock**. All these changes after deposition are called **diagenesis**. It goes up to the boundary of **metamorphism**.

In **compaction**, the weight of the layers above squeezes the sediment together. The grains move closer together, and **pore water** is squeezed out. Clays in particular lose a large part of their pore space. In **cementation**, minerals such as **calcite**, **quartz** or **iron oxides** come out of the pore water. They glue the grains together into solid rock like putty.

Coarse fragments turn into coarse-grained rocks through diagenesis. If the pieces are **angular**, they were hardly transported. The hardened rock is then called **breccia**. **Rounded pebbles** turn into a **conglomerate**. A well-known conglomerate in Switzerland is **Nagelfluh**, from which the Rigi and the Napf, for example, are built.

Plant remains also change during diagenesis. As they are buried deeper, **peat** turns into **lignite** and later into **hard coal**. This process is called **coalification**. With pressure and temperature the carbon content rises, while water and volatile substances escape. At the end of the series is the very carbon-rich **anthracite**.

When solutions rich in magnesium flow through limestone, magnesium replaces part of the calcium. This produces the mineral **dolomite**, CaMg(CO₃)₂; the process is called **dolomitisation**. Dolomite builds large parts of the **Dolomites** in Italy. Under high pressure, calcite is dissolved where grains touch. Insoluble remains such as clay are left behind as dark zigzag lines, the **stylolites**. From about **150 to 200 °C**, typical metamorphic minerals form, and diagenesis then turns into metamorphism.

gewusst: Stylolites look like jagged seams and can often be seen well on polished slabs of limestone.
The Dolomites are named after the mineral dolomite, and the mineral after the French scientist Déodat de Dolomieu.

teile.einleitung: Surf forms when waves break on the coast. The water foams white and sprays up high. Surf is beautiful to look at, but it can also be dangerous.
wichtigste: Surf is waves breaking on the coast.
Waves break because the water gets shallower towards the shore.
The foam is white because it contains many air bubbles.
The fine drops that spray up are called spray.
A rip current can pull swimmers out to sea.
If you get caught in a current, swim sideways, parallel to the beach.

abschnitte.text: Out at sea, the waves roll along evenly. As they approach the shore, the water gets **shallower**. At the bottom, the wave is slowed down by the sea floor. At the top it is faster, gets steeper, tips forwards and **breaks**. This breaking of waves on the coast is called **surf**.

When a wave breaks, a lot of **air** is mixed into the water. The many small bubbles make the foam look **white**. When waves crash against rocks, fine drops of water spray high into the air. These drops are called **spray**. On windy days you can see it flying far across the coast.

The water of the surf has to get back into the sea. It often flows quickly away from the beach in **narrow channels**. This **rip current** can pull swimmers out. The important thing is: stay calm and do not swim straight against the current towards the shore. It is better to swim **sideways, parallel to the beach**. The current is usually only narrow, so you get out of it and can then return to the shore.

The surf is always at work on the coast. The waves roll **stones** back and forth again and again. This grinds off the edges, and the stones become **round**. On cliffs, the surf gnaws at the rock and can carve out caves and rock arches. In a **storm**, the waves are especially high and the surf roars especially wildly.

gewusst: The round pebbles on many beaches were ground smooth by the surf over a long time.
Even on large Swiss lakes such as Lake Constance or Lake Geneva, there can be strong surf in a storm.

teile.einleitung: Gypsum is a soft, widespread mineral. You know it from the hospital, from building sites and from the craft box, but it also forms giant crystals in caves.
wichtigste: Gypsum has a hardness of 2 on the Mohs scale and can be scratched with a fingernail.
It is made of calcium sulphate with water, chemically CaSO4 · 2 H2O.
Burnt gypsum becomes hard again with water.
Alabaster is a fine-grained, translucent kind of gypsum.
Selenite (“Marienglas” in German) is clear gypsum that can be split into sheets.
In the Crystal Cave of Naica in Mexico, gypsum crystals grow over 10 m long.

abschnitte.text: Gypsum is very soft. On the **Mohs scale** it has a hardness of 2. A fingernail is a little harder and can therefore scratch gypsum. Chemically, gypsum is made of **calcium sulphate** and water. The formula is CaSO4 · 2 H2O. The water is firmly built into the crystal; it is called **water of crystallisation**.

If you heat gypsum, it loses part of its water of crystallisation. This produces **burnt gypsum**, also known as plaster of Paris, a white powder. If you mix it with water, it takes the water up again. Firm, tangled crystals form, and the plaster becomes hard. That is why it can easily be poured into moulds.

In **hospital**, a **plaster cast** is put on when a bone is broken. It is put on wet and then becomes hard. In this way it keeps the broken bone still until it has grown back together. On building sites, gypsum is used for wall plaster and plasterboard. Artists and craft lovers also cast figures in plaster.

**Alabaster** is very fine-grained gypsum. It is soft, easy to carve and lets some light through. Figures and vessels are made from it. **Selenite** is the name for large, glass-clear gypsum crystals that can be split into thin sheets. In German it is called “Marienglas” (Mary's glass): in the past, such sheets were placed in front of pictures of the Virgin Mary, which is where the name comes from.

In the dry soils of deserts, gypsum crystals form as flat, petal-like plates. These **desert roses** often contain sand, which gives them their colour. In the mine of **Naica** in Mexico there is a crystal cave. There, in very warm water rich in minerals, gypsum crystals grew more than 10 m long. They are among the largest known crystals in the world.

gewusst: In the Crystal Cave of Naica it is so hot and humid that people can only stay inside for a short time.
Gypsum often forms when seawater evaporates and the dissolved substances are left behind.

teile.einleitung: A glacier mouth is an opening in the ice at the lower end of a glacier. The meltwater flows out of it as a glacial stream. Glacier mouths are impressive, but also dangerous.
wichtigste: The glacier mouth is at the lower end of the glacier.
A stream of meltwater, the glacial stream, flows out of the mouth.
The water is milky grey and is called glacial milk.
Most water flows out on warm summer afternoons.
You must never go into a glacier mouth because ice can break off.
The Rhône rises at the Rhône Glacier near the Furka Pass.

abschnitte.text: A glacier is a huge stream of ice that slowly flows down the valley. **Meltwater** collects under it and inside it. At the lower end, this water comes out through a large opening. This opening is called the **glacier mouth**. Sometimes it is so big that it looks like the entrance to a cave.

The water from the glacier mouth does not look clear, but **milky grey**. As the glacier flows, it grinds over the rock and crushes stone into fine flour. This **rock flour** floats along in the water. That is why the cloudy water is called **glacial milk**. Only in lakes does the flour slowly sink, and the water becomes clearer.

abschnitte.titel: Lots of water in the afternoon
abschnitte.text: How much water flows out of the mouth depends on the weather. When it is warm, a lot of ice melts. That is why the glacial stream carries the most water on **warm summer afternoons**. At night and in winter there is much less. Because the glacier flows and melts away at its end, the mouth changes **from year to year**. It can get bigger, collapse or form in a different place.

A glacier mouth looks exciting, but you should **never go inside**. The ice at the mouth is melting and is often brittle. Large pieces of ice can suddenly fall down. The stream can also swell quickly. That is why it is best to look at a glacier mouth from a safe distance.

Many Swiss rivers begin at a glacier. The **Rhône** rises at the **Rhône Glacier** in Valais, near the Furka Pass. At first its water comes from the glacier's meltwater. From there it flows through Valais into Lake Geneva and on through France to the Mediterranean Sea.

gewusst: At the Rhône Glacier, in summer you can walk through a grotto cut into the ice, which is dug out again every year.
Glacial milk turns some mountain lakes turquoise because the fine rock flour scatters the light.

teile.einleitung: Black ice is a thin, smooth layer of ice on roads and paths. It is dangerous in winter because you can hardly see it and you easily slip on it.
wichtigste: Black ice is a smooth layer of ice on the ground.
It often forms when rain falls on frozen ground.
Black ice is transparent and therefore hard to see.
On bridges the road often freezes first.
Salt or grit is spread to fight black ice.
Taking small steps like a penguin makes you slip less.

abschnitte.text: Water freezes at **zero degrees**. If rain falls on ground that is colder, it freezes into ice straight away. This creates a thin, smooth layer. Black ice can also form when wet roads freeze during the night. At temperatures around zero degrees and below, you must therefore always expect black ice.

Black ice is completely clear and thin, almost like **glass**. You can see the dark ground underneath it and hardly notice the ice. That is what makes it so dangerous. Often the road just looks wet. Cars can start to skid, and people on foot easily fall over.

On **bridges** the road often becomes slippery first. They are cooled by cold air from above and from below. That is why they freeze earlier than the rest of the road. Shady spots and forest roads also often stay icy for longer. Warning signs point out the danger of black ice in such places.

The **winter service** spreads **salt** on the roads. Salt makes the ice melt, even when it is a little below zero degrees. On pavements, **grit** made of tiny stones is often spread. Grit does not melt the ice, but it makes the ground rough so that shoes grip better.

If you have to walk across black ice, it is best to take **small, flat steps** like a penguin. This keeps your weight over your feet, and you slip less. Shoes with a good tread help. **Spikes** or **shoe chains** have small metal points that dig into the ice. Cyclists and drivers should go especially slowly on black ice.

gewusst: At very low temperatures salt hardly works any more; then grit is what helps most.
Penguins walk with small steps and keep their bodies over their feet, which is why they rarely slip.

teile.einleitung: An ensemble forecast is a weather forecast in which a computer model is not run once but many times. Each run starts with slightly changed starting values. This shows how certain or uncertain a forecast is.
wichtigste: An ensemble forecast consists of many model runs with slightly changed starting conditions.
The global ensemble of the ECMWF has 51 members (as of 2025).
The run without any disturbances is called the control run.
A large spread of the members means an uncertain forecast.
In 1963 Edward Lorenz showed that tiny differences at the start can have big effects.
MeteoSwiss runs the ensembles ICON-CH1-EPS and ICON-CH2-EPS.

abschnitte.text: The atmosphere is a **chaotic system**. This means that tiny differences at the start can lead to completely different weather after a few days. The American scientist **Edward Lorenz** discovered this in 1963 using simple weather models. This led to the image of the **butterfly effect**. Because the starting state of the air can never be measured quite exactly, every forecast is a little uncertain.

In an **ensemble forecast**, the computer runs the weather model many times. The **control run** starts with the unchanged analysis, the best known starting state. The other **members** are given small disturbances. The global ensemble of the **ECMWF**, the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, has 51 members: one control run and 50 disturbed runs (as of 2025). Many ensembles also disturb the model physics, to capture errors in the model itself.

If the results of the members lie close together, the forecast is certain. If they go far apart, this is called a large **spread**. Then the forecast is uncertain. **Probabilities** can also be calculated from the ensemble. If, for example, rain falls in 15 of 50 members, this gives a 30 per cent chance of rain.

A well-known way of showing this is the **spaghetti plot**. A particular line, such as a height contour, from all the ensemble members is drawn on top of each other. If the lines lie close together, the weather situation is certain. If they spread out, the picture looks like a plate of spaghetti.

**MeteoSwiss** also runs ensembles. The model **ICON-CH1-EPS** has 11 members and calculates in very fine detail for the next few hours. **ICON-CH2-EPS** has 21 members and reaches several days ahead (as of 2025). Especially in the mountainous terrain of the Alps, such models help to estimate thunderstorms, heavy rain or snowfall better.

gewusst: The ECMWF has its headquarters in Reading in England, and Switzerland is a member.
Lorenz noticed the effect when he repeated a calculation with slightly rounded numbers and got a completely different result.

teile.einleitung: On 11 September 1881, a huge mass of rock crashed down into the valley near Elm in the canton of Glarus. The landslide cost 114 people their lives. One reason for the disaster was the quarrying of slate on the mountain.
wichtigste: Elm lies at the far end of the Sernf Valley in the canton of Glarus.
The landslide happened on 11 September 1881.
About 10 million cubic metres of rock broke away from the Plattenbergkopf.
114 people died and 83 buildings were destroyed.
Slate quarrying had undermined the slope.
The geologist Albert Heim studied the landslide closely.

abschnitte.text: **Elm** lies at the far end of the **Sernf Valley** in the canton of **Glarus**. Today it belongs to the municipality of **Glarus Süd**. In the 19th century the village was known for its **slate**. This rock can be split into thin slabs. Among other things, it was used to make writing slates and slate pencils for schoolchildren.

For years slate was quarried on the slope of the **Plattenbergkopf**. As a result, the mountain was more and more **undermined**. Cracks were already appearing in the rock before the disaster. In September 1881 it rained heavily. Together with the quarrying, this finally made the slope lose its hold.

On 11 September 1881, **two smaller falls** came down first. They attracted curious onlookers. Shortly afterwards came the **main fall**, which hit many of these people. About **10 million cubic metres** of rock crashed several hundred metres down. Then the mass spread out like a stream and flowed about **two kilometres** across the flat valley floor.
**114 people** died in the landslide. In addition, **83 buildings** were destroyed. It was one of the worst landslides in the history of Switzerland. Whole families lost relatives and their homes.

The Swiss geologist **Albert Heim** studied the landslide closely. Together with the pastor **Ernst Buss**, he published a report about it in the same year. His studies had a strong influence on **landslide research**.

gewusst: After falling, the mass of rock at Elm flowed about two kilometres further over flat ground.
Writing slates made of Glarus slate used to be used in many schools.

teile.einleitung: Feldspars are a large group of minerals. They are found in almost all the rocks of the Earth's crust and are important for ceramics, glass and even jewellery.
wichtigste: Feldspars are the most common minerals in the Earth's crust.
They are found in granite, gneiss, basalt and many other rocks.
Orthoclase, a potassium feldspar, stands for hardness 6 on the Mohs scale.
When feldspar weathers, kaolin forms, a raw material for porcelain.
Feldspar is used mainly for ceramics and glass.
Moonstone and labradorite are shimmering feldspars.

abschnitte.text: Feldspars make up a large part of the **Earth's crust**. They are found in igneous rocks such as granite and basalt, but also in gneiss and sandstone. Many stones in Swiss mountains and streams also contain feldspar. The crystals are often white, grey or pink and shine on their smooth faces. Feldspars are made mainly of silicon, oxygen and aluminium, together with potassium, sodium or calcium.

In the past, miners used the word **spar** for minerals that can be split well along smooth surfaces. Feldspar has two such **directions of cleavage**. That is why, if you hit it, it often breaks into pieces with flat faces. Experts distinguish the **potassium feldspars**, which contain potassium, from the **plagioclases**, which contain sodium and calcium.

The scientist Friedrich Mohs sorted minerals by their hardness. As the reference for hardness 6 he chose **orthoclase**, a potassium feldspar. This makes feldspar a little harder than window glass but softer than quartz. Potassium feldspar is often flesh red to pink in colour. If a **granite** contains a lot of it, the whole rock looks reddish.

abschnitte.titel: A raw material for porcelain and glass
abschnitte.text: Over a very long time, water breaks feldspar down. This produces a white clay, **kaolin**. Kaolin is a main ingredient of **porcelain**. Fresh feldspar is also an important raw material: it melts during firing and binds the other ingredients together. That is why it is used for ceramics, tiles and glass.

Some feldspars are popular gemstones. **Moonstone** has fine layers inside that scatter the light. This creates a milky, bluish shimmer. **Labradorite** is named after the Labrador peninsula in Canada. Depending on the angle, it shimmers metallic blue, green or even gold, because light is reflected by fine layers in the crystal.

gewusst: Without feldspar there would be no porcelain, because the kaolin for it forms from weathered feldspar.
The colourful shimmer of labradorite has its own name: labradorescence.

teile.einleitung: An early warning system is meant to warn people of a danger before it arrives. There are systems for earthquakes, tsunamis, debris flows, floods and many other natural hazards.
wichtigste: An effective early warning system needs knowledge of risks, monitoring, spreading of the warning and the ability to respond.
Earthquake warnings use the fast P waves, which arrive before the destructive waves.
Close to the epicentre there is a blind zone where the warning comes too late.
The siren test in Switzerland normally takes place on the first Wednesday in February.
At the Illgraben in Valais, the WSL is testing a warning system for debris flows.
Tsunami warning systems use pressure sensors on the sea floor.

abschnitte.text: According to the **United Nations**, four things belong to an effective early warning system: knowledge about the risks, monitoring with measuring instruments, the spreading of the warning and people's ability to respond correctly. So a network of measuring stations alone is not enough. The warning must reach people, and they must know what to do. The UN's **Sendai Framework** applies from 2015 to 2030 and aims to reduce disaster risks, among other things with more early warning systems.

In an earthquake, the faster **P waves** set off first, followed by the destructive **S waves** and surface waves. Seismometers close to the focus detect the first waves. The warning is sent by radio almost at the speed of light. An example: a place is 70 km away. At 6 km/s the P wave needs about 11.7 seconds, and at 3.5 km/s the S wave about 20 seconds. So about 8 seconds are left. Close to the epicentre lies the **blind zone**, where the warning comes too late.

A **tsunami** lifts the whole column of water in the sea. On the sea floor this can be measured as a small change in pressure. **Pressure sensors** in the deep sea send the values to a buoy. This passes them on by satellite to warning centres. In this way coasts can be warned before the wave arrives.

The **Illgraben** near Leuk produces several debris flows almost every year, that is, streams of water, mud and stones. The Swiss Federal Research Institute **WSL** uses it as a test area. **Geophones** sense the shaking, and radar measures the height of the flow. When the sensors detect a debris flow, warnings are set off at bridges and paths.

There is a dense network of **sirens** in Switzerland. Every year the **siren test** normally takes place on the first Wednesday in February. The general alarm is tested, and below dams the **water alarm** too. During the test, people do not need to do anything. In a real alarm, you should listen to the radio and follow the instructions of the authorities.

gewusst: Japan sends earthquake warnings automatically to mobile phones, often a few seconds before the strong shaking.
The Sendai Framework is named after the Japanese city of Sendai, where it was adopted in 2015.

teile.einleitung: Copernicus is the Earth observation programme of the European Union. Satellites watch the land, sea and atmosphere and provide data for the environment, the climate and disaster protection. The data are free of charge for everyone.
wichtigste: Copernicus is run by the EU; ESA is responsible for the Sentinel satellites.
Before 2012 the programme was called GMES.
Sentinel-1 carries a C-band radar.
Sentinel-2 provides pictures with a resolution of up to 10 metres.
Sentinel-5P measures trace gases such as nitrogen dioxide with TROPOMI.
Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich measures sea level.
The data are freely available to everyone.

abschnitte.text: **Copernicus** is funded and run by the **European Union**. The European Space Agency **ESA** is responsible for the **Sentinel satellites**. Some of them are operated by the weather satellite organisation **EUMETSAT**. The programme used to be called **GMES**, short for Global Monitoring for Environment and Security. In 2012 it was given the name of the astronomer **Nicolaus Copernicus**.

**Sentinel-1** carries a **C-band radar**. Radar sees through clouds and also works at night. The pictures are used, for example, to watch sea ice, floods and **ground movements** with the method called InSAR. **Sentinel-2** measures in 13 spectral channels, the finest with **10 metres** per pixel. Together, two such satellites take a picture of the same place on the equator every **5 days**, and even more often at higher latitudes.

**Sentinel-5P** carries the spectrometer **TROPOMI**. It covers the whole Earth every day and measures **trace gases** such as nitrogen dioxide, ozone, methane and carbon monoxide. **Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich** uses **radar altimetry** to measure the height of the sea surface to within a few centimetres. It continues a series of measurements of global **sea level** that has been running since 1992.

The **Copernicus Emergency Management Service** helps after disasters. After floods, fires or earthquakes, satellite pictures are turned into **damage maps** within hours. These maps help rescue teams with their planning. In this way they can quickly see which roads, bridges or villages are affected.

An **open data policy** applies to the Sentinel data. They are available to everyone **freely and free of charge**. Anyone can download them from online portals. This has led to them being used a lot in research, by authorities and in business. In Switzerland, too, experts use Sentinel pictures to keep track of glaciers, forests or fields, for example.

gewusst: Sentinel-6 is named after the American scientist Michael Freilich, who led NASA's Earth observation.
Radar satellites such as Sentinel-1 can detect ground movements of a few millimetres.

teile.einleitung: The glacier snout, also called the glacier tongue, is the lowest part of a glacier. It reaches down into the valley, long and narrow, and often looks like a tongue sticking out. It shows especially clearly whether a glacier is growing or shrinking.
wichtigste: The glacier snout is the lower end of a glacier.
It lies in the ablation zone, where more ice melts than snow is added.
If more ice melts at the bottom than flows in from above, the snout retreats.
A thick layer of debris protects the ice and slows down melting.
Where the ice flows over a steep step, many crevasses form across it.
Dense ice glows bluish because it absorbs red light.

abschnitte.text: A glacier has two parts. Up in the **accumulation zone**, more snow falls than melts in summer. Over time the snow turns into ice. Further down lies the **ablation zone**. There, more ice melts away each year than new snow is added. The **glacier snout** lies entirely in the ablation zone. It is fed only by the ice that flows down from above.

The ice of a glacier always flows down the valley. Even so, the snout can **retreat**. This happens when more ice melts at its end than comes down from above. A glacier snout reacts to a change in the climate **with a delay**, often only after years or decades. Large glaciers such as the **Great Aletsch Glacier** react especially slowly. For many decades, most glacier snouts in the Alps have been getting shorter.

On many glacier snouts there are stones and rubble. A **thick layer of debris** works like a blanket. It protects the ice from the sun and warm air and so slows down melting. A **thin, dark layer of dust** does the opposite. It absorbs a lot of the sun's heat and makes the ice underneath melt faster.

When the ice flows over a **steep step**, it is stretched and tears open. This creates many **transverse crevasses** running across the direction of flow. Where the ice is very dense and has few air bubbles, it glows **bluish**. Dense ice mainly absorbs red light. What is left is the blue part, which we see.

A glacier snout scours out a deep hollow at the end of the valley. This is called a **tongue basin**. After the last Ice Age, many of these basins filled with water. This is how many lakes in the Alpine foothills formed. At the edge of the snout, debris is also left behind as a ridge: the **moraine**. Old moraines show how far a glacier used to reach.

gewusst: The Great Aletsch Glacier in Valais is the longest glacier in the Alps.
Even though a glacier snout is shrinking, the ice inside it keeps flowing down the valley.

teile.einleitung: Mica is a group of minerals that can be split into wafer-thin, flexible flakes. Mica shines and glitters and is found in many rocks such as granite and gneiss. It is also used in technology and in cosmetics.
wichtigste: Mica can be split into flakes thinner than paper.
Mica belongs to the sheet silicates.
Muscovite is a light, almost colourless mica.
Biotite is a dark, blackish-brown mica.
Mica insulates against electric current and withstands heat.
Mica schist is a rock containing a great deal of mica.

abschnitte.text: The most striking thing about mica is its **cleavage**. It can be split in one direction into wafer-thin flakes. These are thinner than paper, shiny and bendable. The reason lies in its structure: mica belongs to the **sheet silicates**. Its building blocks are joined into flat layers that hold together only weakly.

There are different kinds of mica. **Muscovite** is light, almost colourless and has a silvery shine. In thin flakes it is see-through. **Biotite** is dark, blackish-brown to black. It contains a lot of iron and magnesium. It is named after the French physicist **Jean-Baptiste Biot**. Both kinds of mica are common in granite and gneiss.

In the past, panes of glass were expensive. In Russia, large, see-through sheets of mica were therefore put into windows. This material was called “Muscovy glass”. That is where the name **muscovite** comes from. Small viewing windows in stoves were also made of mica, because it withstands heat well.

Mica **does not conduct electricity** and can cope with high temperatures. That is why it is used for **insulation** in electrical engineering. You find it, for example, in toasters and hairdryers, where hot wires are held in place. Finely ground mica reflects light from its smooth flakes. In eyeshadow or lipstick it gives a **pearly shine** and is often listed as “Mica” on the packaging.

When mudstones are changed by pressure and heat deep inside the Earth, **mica schist** forms. This is a metamorphic rock, which means a rock that has been changed. The mica flakes in it all lie in the same direction. That is why mica schist glitters strongly in the sun. In the Swiss Alps you can find such glittering rocks along many hiking paths.

gewusst: The name muscovite recalls Moscow, because sheets of mica used to be known as “Muscovy glass”.
Glittering grains in the sand of a stream are often mica and not gold.

teile.einleitung: A glacial lake outburst flood is the sudden draining of a lake that is dammed by a glacier or by glacial debris. In a short time a huge amount of water can rush into the valley and cause great damage.
wichtigste: Glacial lakes are dammed by moraines, by glacier ice or by material from rockfalls.
If the dam breaks or the water finds a way under the ice, the lake suddenly empties.
In ice-dammed lakes, the outflow often gets faster and faster because the water melts its channels in the ice wider.
Moraine dams often break when an ice or rock avalanche crashes into the lake and sets off a flood wave.
In Switzerland, Lac des Faverges on the Plaine Morte, the Gornersee and the Märjelensee are well-known examples.
In 1941, the outburst of Laguna Palcacocha in Peru destroyed a large part of the city of Huaraz.

abschnitte.text: When glaciers melt, the water often collects in hollows. It is held back by a natural dam. This can be a **moraine**, a ridge of loose debris that the glacier left behind in the past. The **glacier ice** itself can also block off a side valley. Sometimes a rockfall dams the water. Each of these kinds of dam can give way in its own way.

In an ice-dammed lake, the water finds a way through channels under the glacier. The flowing water creates heat through friction and melts the walls of the channels. Larger channels let more water through, and so the outflow gets **faster and faster**. With a moraine dam, an **avalanche** is often the trigger: if ice or rock crashes into the lake, a flood wave forms. It washes over the loose dam and quickly wears it away.

On the glacier of the **Plaine Morte** lies Lac des Faverges. In many summers it drains under the ice, and the water flows towards **Lenk im Simmental**. At the end of July 2018 this caused flooding in the valley, so in 2019 a channel was cut into the ice. The **Gornersee** on the Gorner Glacier used to empty almost every summer towards Zermatt and was studied closely by experts. At the Great Aletsch Glacier, the **Märjelensee** caused flooding in the Rhône Valley several times, until a drainage tunnel towards the Fiesch Valley was built at the end of the 19th century.

In Peru in 1941, the moraine dam of **Laguna Palcacocha** broke. A flood wave of water and mud destroyed a large part of the city of **Huaraz**, and thousands of people died. In Iceland, the lake **Grímsvötn** lies under the Vatnajökull glacier. There the heat of a volcano melts the ice. When the water level rises high enough, the water lifts the ice barrier and drains away all at once. Such floods are called **jökulhlaups**.

Because the glaciers are shrinking, new lakes are forming in the Alps. Experts therefore watch dangerous lakes closely. The water level is measured, and warning systems are built that sound the alarm if the water suddenly drains. With tunnels, channels or pumps, the water level can be kept low. This means less water flows out in an outburst.

gewusst: At the Märjelensee, a tunnel was built more than a hundred years ago to protect the Rhône Valley.
Under Iceland's Vatnajökull, a volcano uses its heat to fill a lake that empties again and again.

teile.einleitung: In an upwelling zone, cold water rises from the depths of the ocean to the surface. This water brings many nutrients with it. That is why upwelling zones are among the most fertile regions of the seas.
wichtigste: In upwelling, cold deep water replaces surface water that has been carried away.
The deep water is rich in nutrients such as nitrate and phosphate.
The large coastal upwelling zones lie on the west coasts of the continents at low latitudes.
Ekman transport pushes the surface water away from the coast.
There is also upwelling at the equator in the Pacific.
A large part of the world's fish catch comes from upwelling zones.
Deserts such as the Atacama or the Namib often lie on such coasts.

abschnitte.text: The water at the sea surface is usually warmer than the water deep down. When the surface water is pushed away, cold water flows in from below. This process is called **upwelling**. The deep water contains many nutrients such as **nitrate** and **phosphate**, because dead organisms are broken down there. In the upwelling zone, these nutrients reach the sunlight.

On the west coasts of the continents, winds often blow along the coast towards the equator. Because the Earth turns, the moving surface water is deflected sideways. This shift is called **Ekman transport**, named after a Swedish ocean scientist. It carries the water out to the open sea, and cold water wells up from below at the coast. Well-known examples are off **Peru and Chile**, Namibia, California and north-west Africa.

There is also upwelling in the middle of the Pacific at the equator. There the **trade winds** blow westwards on both sides of the equator. Ekman transport deflects the water to the north north of the equator and to the south south of it. So the water moves apart, which experts call **divergence**. Cold deep water rises into the gap that forms.

The many nutrients make a great deal of **plankton** grow. Plankton is food for small fish, which in turn are food for larger animals. Upwelling zones cover only a small part of the sea's surface, but they provide a large part of the world's fish catch. In the Humboldt Current off Peru, the **Peruvian anchovy**, also called anchoveta, lives in huge shoals. It is mainly made into fishmeal and fish oil.

The cold upwelling water cools the air directly above it. Cold air below and warmer air above form a stable layering, a so-called **inversion**. Moist air can then hardly rise, and no rain clouds form. That is why deserts such as the **Atacama** in Chile and the **Namib** in Namibia lie on such coasts. Instead, thick **coastal fog** often forms when moist sea air cools down over the cold water.

gewusst: In Chile the coastal fog is called camanchaca. There people catch water droplets from the fog with large fog nets.
Although the Atacama lies right by the sea, it is one of the driest places on Earth.

teile.einleitung: On 25 July 1855 a severe earthquake shook Upper Valais. The epicentre was in the Visp Valley south of Visp. It is regarded as probably the strongest earthquake in the history of Valais.
wichtigste: The Visp earthquake happened on 25 July 1855.
The epicentre was in the Visp Valley.
Today the magnitude is estimated at about 6.2 to 6.4.
It reached intensity VIII on the European Macroseismic Scale.
It set off a rockfall near St Niklaus.
The main earthquake was followed by many aftershocks.

abschnitte.text: On **25 July 1855** the earth shook in the **Visp Valley**. The epicentre, the place on the surface above the earthquake's source, was south of Visp. Many houses and also **churches** were badly damaged. Today the strength, the **magnitude**, is estimated at about 6.2 to 6.4. This makes it one of the strongest earthquakes in Switzerland in recent centuries.

As well as the magnitude there is the **intensity**. It describes how strongly an earthquake is felt in one place and what damage it causes. On the **European Macroseismic Scale**, the Visp earthquake reached intensity **VIII**. This means heavy damage to buildings. At that time there were no measuring instruments yet, so experts rely on old reports of the damage.

The shaking loosened masses of rock near **St Niklaus**. The only known victim of the earthquake was killed by **falling rocks**. Something also changed underground: in **Visperterminen**, some springs afterwards gave a different amount of water. This is because earthquakes can change the paths that groundwater takes through the rock.

After the main earthquake the earth shook many more times in the Visp Valley. These **aftershocks** worried the people even more. The earthquake was felt **all over Switzerland**. There are also reports from Savoy, northern Italy, the Tyrol and southern Germany.

gewusst: Valais is still the region with the highest earthquake risk in Switzerland today.
About a hundred years earlier, in 1755, a severe earthquake shook the area around Brig.

teile.einleitung: The geological time scale divides the Earth's history of about 4.6 billion years into sections. It reaches from the formation of the Earth to today and has names such as Palaeozoic, Jurassic or Cretaceous. With it, researchers can say exactly when dinosaurs lived or mountains formed.
wichtigste: The Earth is about 4.6 billion years old.
The Earth's history is divided into eons, eras, periods and smaller sections.
The Palaeozoic is followed by the Mesozoic, and then the Cenozoic.
The Jurassic system is named after the Jura mountains in Switzerland and France.
About 252 million years ago the Permian-Triassic mass extinction happened, the largest in the Earth's history.
About 66 million years ago the Cretaceous ended with an asteroid impact.
Radiometric methods such as radiocarbon dating are used to work out the age of samples.

abschnitte.text: The Earth's history is so long that it is divided into sections: **eons**, **eras**, periods and epochs. The longest time, the Precambrian, covers almost 90 per cent of the Earth's history. After that come the **Palaeozoic** (ancient life), the Mesozoic (middle life) and the Cenozoic (recent life). Today we live in the Cenozoic, in the Holocene epoch.

The **Mesozoic** lasted from about 252 to 66 million years ago. It consists of the periods Triassic, **Jurassic** and Cretaceous. The name Jurassic comes from the Jura mountains in Switzerland and France, where limestone rocks from this time are typical. During this time dinosaurs ruled the land and ammonites the seas.

About 252 million years ago, in the **Permian-Triassic mass extinction**, about 90 per cent of all sea species died out. It is regarded as the largest mass extinction in the Earth's history and was probably set off by huge volcanic eruptions in Siberia. About 66 million years ago the Cretaceous ended with an **asteroid impact** in Mexico. After that the dinosaurs died out, and mammals spread.

**Radiometric methods** measure how much of a radioactive substance in a sample has already decayed. **Radiocarbon dating** uses carbon-14, which has a half-life of about 5730 years. After three half-lives, only 12.5 per cent of the original C-14 is left. That is why it is only suitable for young organic samples up to about 50,000 years old; for old rocks, other substances such as uranium are used.

abschnitte.titel: The Earth's history as one day
abschnitte.text: If you imagine the whole history of the Earth as one single day, it becomes clear how young humans are. The first simple living things appear early in the morning. The dinosaurs only show up at about 11 pm. **Modern humans** have only existed for the last few seconds before midnight.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large section of the Earth's history, for example the Mesozoic.
An event in which a great many animal and plant species die out in a short time.
The time after which half of a radioactive substance has decayed.
Working out age using the radioactive carbon C-14.

gewusst: The name Jurassic for a whole period of the Earth's history comes from a mountain range that lies partly in Switzerland.
The crater of the asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs is on the Yucatán peninsula in Mexico.
The oldest mineral grains on Earth, from Australia, are about 4.4 billion years old.

teile.einleitung: A fjord is a long, narrow arm of the sea between steep mountains. Fjords formed when glaciers scooped out deep valleys during the Ice Age and the sea later flowed in.
wichtigste: A fjord is an arm of the sea with salt water.
Glaciers scooped out the valleys of the fjords deeply.
Norway is particularly famous for its fjords.
At about 200 km, the Sognefjord is the longest fjord in Norway.
The Geirangerfjord has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2005.
New Zealand also has many fjords.

abschnitte.text: A **fjord** is a long, narrow arm of the sea that reaches far inland. Steep rock walls often tower up on the left and right. In the fjord there is **seawater**, that is, salt water. At the top, some fresh water from rivers often mixes in. Many fjords are very deep, sometimes deeper than the open sea in front of them.

During the **Ice Age**, huge glaciers flowed through the valleys to the sea. They dug the valleys out deeply and made them wide and steep. A typical cross-section looks like a U. When the glaciers melted, sea level rose, and the sea flowed into the valleys.

The coast of **Norway** has over a thousand fjords. The longest is the **Sognefjord**, at about 200 km. The **Geirangerfjord** is known for its steep walls and waterfalls. It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2005. Many people travel through the fjords by ship.

In the south of **New Zealand**, too, glaciers have shaped fjords. There they are often called “sounds”, like Milford Sound. There are also fjords, for example, in Greenland, Iceland, Canada, Chile and Scotland. In all these places there were large glaciers by the sea during the Ice Age.

No. A real fjord is connected to the sea. With its steep shores, **Lake Lucerne** looks similar, but it is a **freshwater lake**. It also lies in valleys that glaciers dug out. That is why some Swiss lakes remind people of fjords.

gewusst: The word fjord comes from the Scandinavian languages and is related to the English word “ford”.
At its deepest point, the Sognefjord is over 1300 metres deep.

teile.einleitung: In gold panning, people search streams for tiny grains of gold. With a flat pan and water, the heavy gold is separated from the light sand. In Switzerland too, people pan for gold in some streams.
wichtigste: Gold is panned with a flat gold pan.
Gold is much heavier than sand and so stays at the bottom of the pan.
Usually you only find tiny, shiny flakes of gold.
A larger lump of pure gold is called a nugget.
In the Napf area between Bern and Lucerne, many people pan for gold.
From 1848, thousands of people headed to California in the gold rush.

abschnitte.text: For gold panning you need a **gold pan**. This is a flat, round dish. You fill it with sand, gravel and water and carefully swirl the pan back and forth. The water washes the **light sand** and pebbles over the edge. The heavy gold stays at the bottom. At the end, with a bit of luck, you see small yellow dots.

Gold is a very **heavy metal**. A piece of gold weighs much more than a piece of stone or sand of the same size. That is why it sinks to the bottom when you swirl the pan. Gold **does not rust** and does not change in water. Even if it lies in a stream for a very long time, it stays shiny. That makes it easy to recognise.

In a stream you almost always find only **gold flakes**. These are tiny, flat and shiny little plates. A larger natural lump of gold is called a **nugget**. Such finds are very rare in gold panning. You have to watch out for glittering mica or fool's gold. At first glance they look similar, but they are not gold.

The **Napf area** between Bern and Lucerne is especially well known. Streams such as the **Grosse Fontanne** carry fine gold there, which is washed out of the rock of the Napf hills. Many families and clubs try gold panning there. You will not get rich, because the grains are very small. In many places there are rules you have to follow so that the stream and its banks stay protected.

In **1848**, gold was found in California. The find was made on the land of the Swiss emigrant **Johann August Sutter**. Soon thousands of people from all over the world travelled there to get rich. This time is called the **gold rush**. For Sutter himself the gold brought no luck, because the gold seekers took over his land.

gewusst: The California gold rush began on the land of a Swiss man, Johann August Sutter.
Gold still shines even after a very long time in water because it does not rust.

teile.einleitung: Ekman transport describes how the wind moves the water at the surface of the sea. The surprising thing is that, overall, the water does not flow in the direction of the wind but at right angles to it. The reason for this is the rotation of the Earth.
wichtigste: Ekman transport is caused by wind friction and the Coriolis force together.
In the Northern Hemisphere, water is carried at 90 degrees to the right of the wind direction.
In the Southern Hemisphere, the transport goes 90 degrees to the left.
The Ekman spiral shows how the direction of the current turns with depth.
The current gets weaker with increasing depth.
Fridtjof Nansen observed the effect, and Vagn Walfrid Ekman explained it in 1905.

abschnitte.text: When the wind blows over the sea, it drags the top layer of water along with it. Through **friction**, this layer passes the movement on to deeper layers. At the same time the **Coriolis force** is at work. It is caused by the rotation of the Earth and deflects moving water to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere. The interplay of these forces is called **Ekman transport**.

Each deeper layer of water is driven by the layer above it and is deflected further. That is why the direction of the current turns with depth like a spiral. This is called the **Ekman spiral**. At the same time each layer loses momentum through friction, so the current gets weaker further down. According to the ideal theory, the top layer flows at an angle of **45 degrees** to the wind. Averaged over the whole layer, the result is a transport at **90 degrees** to the wind direction.

The Norwegian polar explorer **Fridtjof Nansen** let his ship **Fram** drift in the pack ice of the Arctic Ocean. He noticed that the drifting ice did not move exactly with the wind, but a little to the right of it. In **1905** the Swedish scientist **Vagn Walfrid Ekman** explained this observation mathematically. The effect is named after him.

Ekman transport has big effects. If the wind blows parallel to a coast, it can drive the surface water away from the land out to sea. Then cold, **nutrient-rich deep water** rises. This is called **upwelling**. Such areas, for example off Peru, are particularly rich in fish. In the large **subtropical ocean gyres**, Ekman transport carries water towards the middle. Floating **plastic waste** collects there, for example in the Great Pacific Garbage Patch.

gewusst: Below about one hundred metres deep, you can often hardly feel the wind-driven current at all.
Nansen's Fram expedition lasted from 1893 to 1896.

teile.einleitung: Fossils are remains or traces of living things that lived a very long time ago and were preserved in rock. Thanks to them we know what dinosaurs, ancient fish or ammonites looked like. They are like windows into the Earth's past.
wichtigste: Fossils are the petrified remains or traces of living things from prehistoric times.
They are found most often in sedimentary rocks.
Ammonites were sea creatures with a spiral shell.
The science that studies fossils is called palaeontology.
Monte San Giorgio in Ticino is a UNESCO World Heritage Site because of its fossils.
Fossils help to work out the age of layers of rock.

abschnitte.text: A **fossil** is the remains of a living thing that is older than about 10,000 years. It can be bones, teeth, shells, leaves of plants or whole imprints. **Trace fossils** such as footprints or feeding tunnels count too. The word comes from the Latin fossilis and means “dug up”.

Usually an animal or a plant dies and is quickly covered by mud or sand. Over a long time these layers are pressed into **sedimentary rock**.
